water.latent_heat_kj_l_reason: Rounded 2257 kJ/kg latent heat at 100 C, taking 1 litre as 1 kg. Grimwood, Fire-fighting Flow-rate, January 2005, p.24, example 2. https://highrisefire.co.uk/docs/FLOW-RATE%20202004.pdf
water.sensible_heat_kj_l_reason: Rounded 4.183 kJ/kg/K times 80 K from 20 C to 100 C, with 1 litre approximated as 1 kg. Same source, p.24; its worked example starts at 18 C. Combined budget is 2590 kJ/litre.
water.application_efficiency_reason: Selected 50 percent effective hose-stream cooling, following Grimwood 2005, pp.26 to 28, especially example 6 for a jet nozzle. This is an estimate for this nozzle, not a measurement. https://highrisefire.co.uk/docs/FLOW-RATE%20202004.pdf
water.wet_seconds_per_litre_reason: Scenario estimate of 30 seconds of ignition inhibition per litre delivered to a cell, additive after the last application. NISTIR 6191 motivates fuel cooling and surface contact, but does not measure this dry-out coefficient. https://www.nist.gov/publications/fire-fighting-properties-nistir-6191 The dry-out credit is banked over a whole spray and counts from its end (a cell under a running spray is wet); before 23 Oct the spray's own seconds used up the credit, which left a wide cone about 0 s of protection. It does not clamp the reheated surface to the boiling point or solve evaporation.
water._reason: Flow is shared over visible cone cell centres: burning_first_share of it over the burning ones, the rest equally over all of them, including cold fuel. Tick-interval overlap conserves litres for non-grid times. Exact room boundaries block water except within current door widths; no furniture occlusion. Flame heat is absorbed first; surplus cools toward ambient using gas.effective_heat_capacity_kj_m2_k times cell area, the existing effective heated-lining capacity. There is no separate solid-cell capacity in this model. Smoke and room gas use the remaining heat release. Wetting is a dry-out timer, not moisture transport or a validated suppression model. Sources accessed 2026-10-21.
water.extinction_reason: Retained heat and displayed flame may reach zero while fuel remains hot. Extinguish only when a positive delivered water budget absorbs the full step heat release and the remaining cooling takes the fuel below its material ignition temperature. Extinguished fuel stops consuming mass. It can ignite again only when dry and heated by neighbours or room gas. The unquenched combustion ramp is independent of displayed flame. Mechanisms: Grimwood, Fire-fighting Flow-rate, January 2005, p.6, fuel and flame cooling; pp.24 and 26 to 28, water heat capacity and stream efficiency, https://highrisefire.co.uk/docs/FLOW-RATE%20202004.pdf . Stroup and Madrzykowski, Fire Fighting Properties, NISTIR 6191, July 1998, chapter 2, https://www.nist.gov/publications/fire-fighting-properties-nistir-6191 . The strict ignition-temperature extinction criterion is a model rule supported by these mechanisms, not an experimentally fitted extinction law.
water.burning_first_share_reason: Share of a stream aimed at flames that lands on the burning cells of its cone; the rest wets the whole cone. A crew aims a direct attack at the base of the flames (IFSTA Essentials, fire streams), and spray_water is only allowed toward a hot spot the robot's own scan found within aim_tolerance_deg. 0.7 is an engineering choice for a narrow fog pattern, not a measured value; application_efficiency still counts the water lost as steam and run-off. Issue list 23 Oct, item 7: water shared evenly over every visible cell of a 5 m cone mostly fell on floor that was not burning.
water.quench_keeps_growth_share_reason: A cell water put out keeps its share of its origin's alpha t^2 growth budget while it stays out, so the growth cap does not hand that share to the cells still burning. Without it, a fire with the cap binding returned to exactly its budget after water put out most of its cells, which no fire model does: FDS reduces the burning rate where water lands and moves no heat elsewhere (FDS Technical Reference Guide, reduction of pyrolysis rate due to water).

spread.growth_alpha_kw_s2_reason: Medium design-fire coefficient per independent configured origin. NFPA 72, National Fire Alarm Code, 2002 edition, Annex B, pp.72-168 to 72-169, equations B.4/B.5 give Q=alpha*(t-tv)^2 and alpha=1055/tg^2; choosing tg=300 s gives 0.0117222, rounded here to the requested 0.01172 kW/s^2, or 1054.8 kW at 300 s. https://previewnorm.com/nfpa/NFPA%2072-2002%20PDF.pdf . One budget is shared by all cells descended from that origin, across rooms. Mass loss cannot exceed burning fuel capacity. Step energy integrates the quadratic exactly. Zero explicitly selects the legacy uncapped model for diagnostic configurations; older files without this field retain that behaviour. No growth clock ignites a new room. Accessed 2026-10-23.

sources.justification: 0.25 m grid and 0.1 s step are numerical choices. One sofa ignition at (3,1.25) m at 0 s with radius 0.3 m is an estimated scenario choice. Furniture footprints are estimates, clipped to their room. Surface names and landmark kinds come from floorplan.json and props.json. All room boundaries must align to the grid.

20 C ambient is a scenario choice. NIST describes flashover with fire gases over 600 C and about 20 kW/m2 floor heat flux. Use 600 C as a gas-temperature trigger. 650 to 1100 C flame temperature and 1100 C hard bound are selected plausible ranges, not material-specific measurements. Flashover timing depends on ventilation and contents; no flashover time is forced. The earlier 180 to 300 s calibration target is retired in favour of medium t-squared origin growth.

USDA Wood Handbook chapter 18 gives 300 to 400 C surface temperatures before piloted wood ignition. Wood values of 330 C use that range. Other ignition values and every fuel density are estimates, documented in each material. No source certifies these particular household objects.

CFAST motivates hot upper and cooler lower room layers; this code does not implement CFAST. Every coefficient is estimated. Effective heat capacity 6.5 kJ/m2/K includes entrained gas and heated linings. Loss 0.055 kW/m2/K is an effective room heat loss. Convective heat fraction 0.65, exchange 3.5 internal and 0.4 external m3/s per metre of opening, gas capacity 1.2 kJ/m3/K, entrainment 0.0012 m3/s/kW are coarse choices. Initial layer depth 0.05 m and minimum height 0.4 m avoid zero volume. Lower heat fraction 0.12 and lower smoke fraction 0.08 preserve stratification. Smoke production 0.012 density*m3 per full-intensity burning cell per second, reference volume 1 m3 and decay 0.002/s define a dimensionless visual density, not soot concentration or visibility. Door exchange is multiplied by the fraction of the opening below the lower of the two layer interfaces; no hot gas crosses above a door head. The 3.5 value corresponds to a few m/s in a 2.1 m high opening and is an estimate. Heat capacity and exchange were selected using standalone default-house timing diagnostics, not experiments.

NIST experiments establish that upholstery and construction details change growth; they do not supply these coefficients. All spread constants are estimates: neighbour exchange 0.028/s, cooling 0.012/s, effective upper-gas radiation coupling 0.05/s, post-flashover heating 18 C/s, burn flux 0.018 kg/m2/s, ramp 8 s, relaxation 4 s, fuel variation +/-8%, effective heat of combustion 18000 kJ/kg. Query heating takes the maximum contribution of nearby same-room flames, with inverse-square horizontal falloff clipped at 1.5 m and a vertical plume scale 1.5 m. Peak added heating 450 C is an estimate. A half door uses half its opening width; closed doors have no leakage or failure. Surface radiation uses upper-layer gas temperature even when the lower air stays cooler; 0.05/s is an estimated 20 s thermal response for exposed finishes and furnishings.

650 C for 45 continuous seconds, six events total and at least 8 s between events are unvalidated ceiling-panel scenario rules, not a structural failure correlation. The 0.9 m protected width follows the floorplan clear-path rule. Only plaster ceilings may shed panels; collapse does not consume fuel or remove walls.

sources.edition: NFPA 72, National Fire Alarm Code, 2002 edition
sources.justification: Annex B equations B.4 and B.5 prescribe quadratic growth after established burning; the medium classification includes 300 s to 1055 kW. The selected coefficient 0.01172 kW/s^2 gives 1054.8 kW at 300 s. This is a design-fire choice, not a claim that every residential fire has this growth rate.
